You are an independent classifier in a blinded experiment about a book of
biblical symbolism. The consensus responses below were produced without access
to the book. Compare them with the book's entry.

TERM
Faithful Witness

BLIND CONSENSUS RESPONSES
RESPONSE A
{
  "primary_meaning": "In mainstream Christian teaching, 'Faithful Witness' (Greek: ho martys ho pistos) is understood primarily as a Christological title: it designates Jesus Christ as the one who perfectly and reliably testifies to God's truth and character — revealing God, confirming God's promises, and remaining true to that testimony even to the point of death. The title carries the double sense of the Greek word martys: 'witness' in the legal/testimonial sense and, by extension, 'martyr,' since Christ's witness culminated in his crucifixion. His resurrection ('firstborn of the dead' in the same verse) vindicates that witness.",

    "Revelation 1:5 — 'Jesus Christ, the faithful witness, the firstborn of the dead, and the ruler of the kings of the earth'",
    "Revelation 3:14 — 'the Amen, the faithful and true witness'",
    "Revelation 19:11 — the rider called 'Faithful and True'",
    "John 18:37 — 'for this purpose I have come into the world, to bear witness to the truth'",
    "John 3:11, 3:32-33 — Jesus testifies to what he has seen; whoever receives his testimony certifies that God is true",
    "1 Timothy 6:13 — Christ Jesus 'who in his testimony before Pontius Pilate made the good confession'",
    "Psalm 89:37 — 'a faithful witness in the skies,' frequently cited as the Old Testament background for Revelation 1:5 via the Davidic covenant context of Psalm 89",

  ],
  "alternatives": [
    {
      "meaning": "Martyrological/ecclesial reading: 'faithful witness' as a designation for believers who testify to Christ faithfully, especially unto death. Antipas is explicitly called 'my faithful witness' (Revelation 2:13), and the term is extended to the church's vocation of costly testimony (Revelation 6:9; 11:3; 12:11; 17:6). This reading treats Christ's faithful witness as the pattern the church is called to imitate.",

        "Revelation 2:13 (Antipas, 'my faithful witness')",
        "Revelation 6:9",
        "Revelation 11:3 (the two witnesses)",
        "Revelation 12:11",
        "Revelation 17:6"
      ],
      "prominence": "common"

      "meaning": "Davidic-covenantal/messianic reading: 'faithful witness' in Revelation 1:5 is read as a deliberate allusion to Psalm 89 (vv. 27, 37), presenting Jesus as the fulfillment of the Davidic covenant — the enduring, guaranteed heir whose throne is as sure as the 'faithful witness in the skies.' Common in academic commentary (e.g., Beale, Bauckham) and complements rather than replaces the primary reading.",

        "Psalm 89:27, 89:37",
        "Revelation 1:5 (parallel triad: witness, firstborn, ruler of kings, echoing Psalm 89)",
        "Isaiah 55:4"
      ],
      "prominence": "common"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "Astronomical/creational reading of Psalm 89:37 itself: the 'faithful witness in the sky' is the moon (or the rainbow, in some older interpretations) as a perpetual natural testimony to God's covenant faithfulness, not a messianic title. This concerns the Psalm's original sense rather than the New Testament title.",
      "basis": [
        "Psalm 89:37 in its immediate context (vv. 36-37, sun and moon as fixed guarantees)",
        "Genesis 9:12-17 (rainbow as covenant sign, in the minority 'rainbow' variant)"
      ],
      "prominence": "minority"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "Prophetic-office reading: 'faithful witness' emphasizes Christ as the true prophet whose testimony contrasts with false witnesses and false prophets (drawing on the wisdom contrast of Proverbs 14:5, 25), and grounds the reliability of the entire revelation given in the Apocalypse — i.e., the title functions to certify the trustworthiness of the book's message.",
      "basis": [
        "Proverbs 14:5, 14:25",
        "Revelation 22:6, 22:16, 22:20 ('these words are trustworthy and true')",
        "Revelation 3:14"
      ],
      "prominence": "minority"
    }
  ],
  "has_settled_consensus": true,
  "confidence": "high",
  "notes": "There is broad, cross-traditional agreement (Catholic, Orthodox, Protestant, and academic biblical scholarship) that 'Faithful Witness' is first and foremost a title of Jesus Christ from Revelation 1:5 and 3:14, denoting his reliable testimony to God vindicated through death and resurrection. The listed alternatives are largely complementary emphases rather than rival meanings: the martyrological/ecclesial extension and the Davidic-covenant background are both widely affirmed alongside the primary Christological sense. Genuine disagreement is limited to secondary questions, such as how strongly the 'martyr' connotation should be pressed in the first-century usage of martys, and what the 'faithful witness in the skies' denotes within Psalm 89 itself."
}

  "has_settled_consensus": true,

  "notes": "When capitalized and used as a biblical title, “Faithful Witness” is overwhelmingly understood as referring to Jesus Christ, especially from Revelation 1:5 and 3:14. There is less uniformity over which aspect is primary—truthful revelation, covenant fidelity, testimony before death, or martyrdom—but these are usually treated as complementary nuances rather than competing identifications."

BOOK ENTRY
The Messiah — the one who bears the Father's light unchanged through the night; the moon is that name written in the sky, His throne established in the heavens.

BOOK'S COMMON-VIEW NOTE, IF PRESENT
(none)

SCRIPTURE REFERENCES PRINTED WITH THE ENTRY
(Ps 89:37; Rev 1:5; 3:14; Isa 55:4) · see Sun, Moon & Stars, ch. 29

AVAILABLE KJV EXCERPTS
Psalms 89:37 — It shall be established for ever as the moon, and as a faithful witness in heaven. Selah.
Revelation 1:5 — And from Jesus Christ, who is the faithful witness, and the first begotten of the dead, and the prince of the kings of the earth. Unto him that loved us, and washed us from our sins in his own blood,
Revelation 3:14 — And unto the angel of the church of the Laodiceans write; These things saith the Amen, the faithful and true witness, the beginning of the creation of God;
Isaiah 55:4 — Behold, I have given him for a witness to the people, a leader and commander to the people.

CLASSIFY THE RELATIONSHIP

First reduce both readings to their minimum core identifications. Do not let
extra detail create an artificial disagreement.

- MATCH: the core identifications are equivalent. Differences are merely
  wording or immaterial detail.
- REFINED: the book preserves the consensus's general referent or category but
  materially changes its extension, boundary, conditions, or precision. A
  narrowing may reject some cases the broader consensus admits; a broadening
  may admit cases it excludes. This is real disagreement at the boundary, but
  not replacement of the central referent.
- DIVERGENT: the cores materially contradict. Both claims cannot be true of the
  same referent in the same context and sense; accepting the book requires
  rejecting or replacing the consensus identification. A source and its
  product remain different referents when the book explicitly denies their
  identity, even if they are causally related.
- NOVEL: no recognizable consensus or listed alternative covers the book's
  core identification. Novelty is absence from consensus, not contradiction.

Use `core_relation` to expose the relationship at the center and
`extension_relation` to expose disagreement over the cases covered. A REFINED
verdict must state what cases the book adds, excludes, or reclassifies. A
DIVERGENT verdict must identify a replaced referent or material contradiction,
not merely a narrower boundary.

Treat the two axes independently. A core-divergent reading may still retain
some cases covered by the consensus while rejecting its central identification;
therefore DIVERGENT does not require disjoint extensions. Conversely, a
narrowed extension is REFINED only when the consensus's central referent or
category remains intact.

Also judge whether the citations printed with the glossary entry alone provide
strong, partial, or insufficient support. Do not yet decide whether a divergent
full chapter is persuasive; that is a separate stage.
